decks.title: Control and Coordination — Part 1: The nervous system
goals: Explain why multicellular organisms need control and coordination
Draw and label a neuron and describe how an impulse crosses a synapse
Distinguish voluntary, involuntary and reflex actions and trace a reflex arc
State the functions of the forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain and spinal cord, and how they are protected

slides.heading: Control and Coordination
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how your body senses a change, sends a message and responds in a fraction of a second.

visual.alt: Flow from a stimulus to a receptor, along nerves to the brain or spinal cord, then to an effector that produces a response

slides.narration: Namaste! Imagine a cricket ball flying towards you. In less than a second your eyes spot it, your brain judges its speed, and your hands move to catch it. Dozens of muscles work together, each at the right moment. This teamwork is called coordination. In this part we discover the system that makes it possible: the nervous system, with its neurons, reflexes, brain and spinal cord.

slides.heading: Why living things need coordination
slides.body_md: A **stimulus** is a change in the surroundings, such as heat, light, sound or touch. Living things respond to stimuli in a controlled way. **Control and coordination** make sure the right body parts act together, at the right time, in the right amount.

rows: Needs many muscles to work together

visual.alt: Table of stimuli and the coordinated responses they cause, with the reason each response helps

slides.narration: Every moment, your surroundings change. It gets hot or cold, bright or dark, noisy or quiet. A living body cannot react randomly. If you touched a hot tava and your legs moved instead of your hand, you would be burnt. So the body needs a system that senses the change and makes exactly the right parts respond. In animals, two systems share this job: the nervous system and the hormonal system.

slides.heading: Receptors: the body’s sensors
slides.body_md: **Receptors** are specialised cells, usually in sense organs, that detect a stimulus and start a message. Each kind of receptor responds to one kind of stimulus.

visual.alt: Table of receptors, the sense organ each is found in and the stimulus each detects

slides.narration: Your body has its own set of sensors. Photoreceptors in the eye respond to light. Receptors in the ear respond to sound. Olfactory receptors in the nose pick up smells, and gustatory receptors in the taste buds pick up tastes. The skin is full of receptors for touch, heat, cold and pain. When a receptor is stimulated, it starts a message that travels along nerve cells.

slides.heading: The neuron: a cell built to carry messages
slides.body_md: A **neuron** (nerve cell) is the unit of the nervous system. Its **dendrites** pick up information, the **cell body** contains the nucleus, the long **axon** carries the impulse, and the **nerve endings** pass it on.

slides.narration: Look at the shape of a neuron. It is long and thin, a little like an electric wire with branched ends. The short branches, called dendrites, collect information. The cell body, with its nucleus, keeps the cell alive. The long axon carries the message, and the nerve endings at the far end hand it over. Some axons in your legs are almost a metre long.

slides.heading: How a nerve impulse travels
slides.body_md: At the dendrite tips, a stimulus sets off a chemical reaction that creates an **electrical impulse**. The impulse travels from the dendrite to the cell body, along the axon, to the nerve ending.

visual.alt: Flow of a nerve impulse: dendrite tip, cell body, axon, nerve ending

slides.narration: Inside a neuron, information travels as a tiny electrical signal called a nerve impulse. It always moves the same way: from the dendrite, into the cell body, along the axon and out to the nerve ending. Remember the order with a simple phrase: dendrites receive, axons send. Exam answers often lose marks because the direction is written backwards.

slides.heading: Crossing the gap: the synapse
slides.body_md: Neurons do not touch. Between the nerve ending of one neuron and the dendrite of the next is a tiny gap, the **synapse**. The electrical impulse makes the nerve ending release **chemicals**, which cross the gap and start a new electrical impulse in the next neuron.

slides.narration: If neurons do not touch, how does the message jump across? Think of a relay race where runners cannot hand over the baton directly, so they throw a ball across a small gap instead. At the end of the axon, the electrical impulse releases chemicals. They drift across the synapse and start a fresh impulse in the next dendrite. The same kind of junction passes messages from neurons to muscles and glands.

slides.heading: Voluntary, involuntary and reflex actions
slides.body_md: Actions can be sorted by whether we think about them.
columns:
**Voluntary** — done by choice, after thinking; controlled by the **forebrain**. Examples: writing, talking, kicking a ball.

**Involuntary** — happen on their own, without our choice; controlled mainly by the **midbrain and hindbrain**. Examples: heartbeat, breathing, salivation.

**Reflex action** — a sudden, automatic response to a stimulus, without conscious thought; usually controlled by the **spinal cord**. Examples: pulling the hand away from a flame, pulling the foot off a sharp stone.

visual.alt: Table comparing voluntary, involuntary and reflex actions by thinking involved, controlling part and an example

slides.narration: Some actions you choose, like writing your name. These are voluntary. Some happen all the time without your choice, like your heartbeat. These are involuntary. And some happen suddenly when you are in danger, like snatching your hand away from a candle flame before you even think. These are reflex actions. Reflexes are the body’s emergency shortcuts.

slides.heading: The reflex arc
slides.body_md: The pathway of a reflex is a **reflex arc**: **receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → effector** (muscle or gland). The connection is made in the spinal cord, so the response is very quick. The message also travels on to the brain.

slides.narration: Here is the shortcut. The receptor in the skin fires an impulse along a sensory neuron into the spinal cord. There, a relay neuron passes it straight to a motor neuron, which makes the muscle contract. The brain is not asked first. That saves precious time. A copy of the message still goes up to the brain, which is why you feel the pain a moment after you have already moved.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: tracing a reflex in the kitchen
slides.body_md: Meera’s finger touches a hot pressure-cooker lid and she pulls her hand back instantly. Trace the reflex arc and explain why she feels the pain only afterwards.
bullets: Step 1 — **Stimulus**: heat. **Receptor**: heat and pain receptors in the skin of the finger.
Step 2 — The **sensory neuron** carries the impulse to the **spinal cord**.
Step 3 — A **relay neuron** in the spinal cord passes it to a **motor neuron**.
Step 4 — The motor neuron reaches the arm **muscle (effector)**, which contracts and pulls the hand away.
Step 5 — The impulse also travels up to the brain; it arrives slightly later, so the pain is felt after the hand has moved.

nodes.label: Brain: pain felt a moment later

visual.alt: Flow tracing the reflex from heat to skin receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron and arm muscle, with a branch to the brain

slides.narration: Let us trace it step by step, the way examiners like. Name the stimulus and the receptor first. Then follow the impulse along the sensory neuron to the spinal cord, across the relay neuron, out along the motor neuron, and into the muscle. Finally, explain the delay in feeling pain: the message to the brain travels further, so awareness comes after the action.

slides.heading: Central and peripheral nervous system
slides.body_md: The **central nervous system (CNS)** is the **brain** and the **spinal cord**. The **peripheral nervous system (PNS)** is made of **cranial nerves** (from the brain) and **spinal nerves** (from the spinal cord), which connect the CNS to every part of the body.

visual.alt: Tree: the nervous system divides into the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves)

slides.narration: Think of the central nervous system as the head office and the peripheral nerves as the telephone lines to every branch. The brain and spinal cord receive information from all over the body, process it and send out instructions. Cranial nerves start from the brain and serve the head, while spinal nerves start from the spinal cord and serve the rest of the body.

slides.heading: The human brain
slides.body_md: The brain has three regions: the **forebrain**, the **midbrain** and the **hindbrain**. The hindbrain includes the **cerebellum**, the **pons** and the **medulla**, which continues as the spinal cord.

slides.narration: The brain is the main coordinating centre of the body. The large, folded forebrain sits on top. Below it lies the small midbrain. At the back and bottom is the hindbrain, made of the cerebellum, the pons and the medulla. The medulla runs down into the spinal cord. The pea-sized pituitary gland hangs just below the brain; we will meet it again with hormones.

slides.heading: The forebrain: thinking and voluntary action
slides.body_md: The **forebrain (cerebrum)** is the main thinking part. It has areas that receive sensations — sight, hearing, smell, touch — and areas that control **voluntary muscles**. It also stores memory and links information to decide what to do.

rows: Combine information with memory to decide
Choosing the right answer in a quiz

visual.alt: Table of forebrain areas, their jobs and everyday examples

slides.narration: When you smell jalebis frying, the impulse reaches a smell area of the forebrain. Another area remembers how sweet jalebis taste, and you decide to buy some. Then the forebrain sends instructions to your leg muscles to walk to the stall. Sensing, remembering, deciding and moving on purpose are all jobs of the forebrain.

slides.heading: The midbrain and hindbrain: automatic control
slides.body_md: Many involuntary actions are controlled by the **midbrain** and **hindbrain**. The **medulla** controls blood pressure, salivation and vomiting. The **pons** helps regulate breathing. The **cerebellum** keeps **posture and balance** and makes voluntary movements **precise**.

rows: Some involuntary actions and reflex movements of the head and eyes

visual.alt: Table of the medulla, pons, cerebellum and midbrain with the region each belongs to and what it controls

slides.narration: You never have to remind yourself to keep your blood pressure steady or to make saliva when food arrives. The medulla in the hindbrain looks after these. The cerebellum is the body’s balance expert. Walking along a narrow wall, riding a cycle, or threading a needle all need the cerebellum to make your movements smooth and accurate.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which part of the brain?
slides.body_md: Decide which part of the brain is mainly involved in each situation.
bullets: Step 1 — Ravi walks along a narrow railway platform edge without falling → balance → **cerebellum** (hindbrain).
Step 2 — Saliva comes into Anu’s mouth when she sees pani puri → salivation → **medulla** (hindbrain).
Step 3 — Kiran solves a sudoku and writes the numbers → thinking and voluntary action → **forebrain**.
Step 4 — Check: thinking or choosing points to the forebrain; balance and precision to the cerebellum; automatic body functions to the medulla.

visual.alt: Worked table matching three situations to the function involved and the brain part responsible

slides.narration: Here is a method that works every time. First, name the function hidden in the situation: is it balance, an automatic body function, or thinking and choosing? Then match the function to the brain part. Balance means cerebellum. Automatic functions like saliva and blood pressure mean medulla. Thinking and voluntary movement mean forebrain.

slides.heading: Quick check: a fall from a cycle
slides.body_md: After a head injury, a cyclist can think and speak clearly but cannot keep his balance or pick up a pen precisely. Which part of the brain is most likely affected?
slides.narration: Quick check. Thinking and speaking are fine, so rule out the thinking part. Which part looks after balance and precise movement?

slides.heading: Protecting the brain and spinal cord
slides.body_md: The brain sits inside a bony box, the **skull (cranium)**, cushioned by **fluid** that absorbs shocks. The spinal cord runs inside the **vertebral column** (backbone).

visual.alt: Table showing the brain protected by the skull and fluid, and the spinal cord by the vertebral column

slides.narration: The brain is soft and delicate, so the body packs it carefully, just as a shopkeeper packs eggs in a padded box. The hard skull keeps out bumps, and a cushion of fluid inside stops the brain from hitting the bone. The spinal cord is threaded through the backbone. This is also why helmets and seat belts matter: they add one more layer of protection.

slides.heading: From impulse to movement
slides.body_md: When a motor neuron’s impulse reaches a muscle, special **proteins** in the muscle cells change their shape and arrangement. The muscle cells **shorten**, and the body part moves.

nodes.label: Impulse arrives along the motor neuron
Muscle proteins change shape and arrangement

visual.alt: Flow from an impulse reaching a muscle to proteins changing shape, the muscle shortening and the body part moving

slides.narration: How does an electrical message become movement? At the junction between nerve and muscle, chemicals are released, just as at a synapse. Inside the muscle cells, special proteins respond by changing their shape and the way they are arranged. The cells become shorter, the muscle pulls on the bone, and your arm bends. Every movement you make, even a blink, works this way.

slides.heading: Limits of electrical impulses
slides.body_md: Nerve impulses are fast, but they reach **only cells connected by nerves**. After firing, a cell needs time to **reset** before it can fire again. So the body also uses **chemical messengers (hormones)**, carried by the blood to all cells.

visual.alt: Table comparing nerve impulses and hormones by speed, reach, how long the effect lasts and typical use

slides.narration: Nerve impulses are like phone calls: very fast, but they only reach houses that have a phone line. Hormones are like a radio broadcast: slower, but anyone with a receiver can pick them up. A neuron also needs a short rest after each impulse. For slow, widespread jobs like growth, the body therefore uses hormones. That is the bridge to Part 2.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: how fast is a reflex?
slides.body_md: In a withdrawal reflex, the impulse travels $0.8\ \text{m}$ from a toe to the spinal cord and $0.8\ \text{m}$ back to the leg muscle. Nerve impulses here travel at $80\ \text{m/s}$. Find the time taken for conduction.
bullets: Step 1 — Total distance $= 0.8 + 0.8 = 1.6\ \text{m}$.
Step 2 — Time $= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} = \dfrac{1.6}{80} = 0.02\ \text{s}$.
Step 3 — In milliseconds: $0.02 \times 1000 = 20\ \text{ms}$.
Check — a message to the brain and back would travel much further, so a reflex is faster than a decision made by the brain.

visual.alt: Worked table: total path 1.6 metres at 80 metres per second takes 0.02 seconds, or 20 milliseconds

slides.narration: Let us put numbers on the speed of a reflex. Add the two distances to get one point six metres. Divide by the speed, eighty metres per second, to get two hundredths of a second, which is twenty milliseconds. Real reflexes take a little longer because each synapse adds a tiny delay. Still, it is far quicker than sending the message all the way to the brain and waiting for a decision.

slides.heading: Summary: the nervous system
bullets: Receptors detect stimuli; effectors (muscles and glands) carry out responses.
A neuron: dendrite → cell body → axon → nerve ending; impulses are electrical inside, chemical across the synapse.
Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron (spinal cord) → motor neuron → effector.
CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = cranial and spinal nerves.
Forebrain: thinking and voluntary actions. Medulla: blood pressure, salivation, vomiting. Cerebellum: balance and precision.
Skull and fluid protect the brain; the vertebral column protects the spinal cord.

rows: Passes the message on by chemicals, one way
Reflex arcs; link between brain and body

visual.alt: Summary table of the neuron, synapse, spinal cord, forebrain and hindbrain with their key jobs

slides.narration: Let us recap. Receptors sense, nerves carry, the brain or spinal cord decides, and effectors act. Inside a neuron the message is electrical; across a synapse it is chemical, and it goes one way only. Reflexes use a short cut through the spinal cord. The forebrain thinks, the hindbrain runs the automatic jobs and keeps you balanced, and bone and fluid keep it all safe.

slides.heading: Exam tips: nervous system
bullets: Write the impulse direction correctly: **dendrite → cell body → axon → nerve ending**.
In a reflex arc, name all five parts in order and say the connection is in the **spinal cord**.
Do not write that reflexes involve "no brain at all"; the brain is informed, but it does not make the response.
Neuron diagram (2 marks usually): dendrite, cell body, nucleus, axon, nerve ending, plus an arrow for direction.
Match functions precisely: blood pressure and salivation → **medulla**; balance → **cerebellum**.
Typical 3-mark split: definition (1) + labelled pathway or diagram (1) + reason or example (1).

rows: Dendrite to cell body to axon to nerve ending
Forebrain controls thinking; cerebellum controls balance
Synapse is a gap crossed by chemicals
The brain is informed, after the response

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes about the nervous system and the correct ideas

slides.narration: Here is how to pick up easy marks. Always draw an arrow showing the direction of the impulse on a neuron. In a reflex arc question, list all five parts in order and mention the spinal cord. Avoid saying the brain plays no part in a reflex; it is informed, just not in charge of the response. And learn the brain functions as exact pairs.

slides.heading: Coordination in plants and hormones in animals
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how plants respond without a nervous system, and how chemical messengers coordinate both plants and animals.

nodes.label: Plants: chemical signals and changes in cells

visual.alt: Flow showing a stimulus leading to a coordinated response through chemical signals in plants and nerves and hormones in animals

slides.narration: Plants have no brain, no nerves and no muscles. Yet a sunflower faces the sun, a money plant climbs a wall, and a seed always sends its root down. How do they do it? In this part we explore how plants respond, then meet the hormones that act as chemical messengers in both plants and animals.

slides.heading: Two kinds of movement in plants
slides.body_md: Plants respond in two ways: **immediate movements** that do not involve growth, and slow **growth movements** in which one side of an organ grows more than the other.

rows: Cells change shape by gaining or losing water

visual.alt: Table comparing immediate plant responses with growth movements by speed, growth, mechanism and example

slides.narration: Some plant movements are fast. Touch a touch-me-not plant and its leaves fold within seconds. No growth can be that quick. Other movements are slow, like a shoot turning to face a window over a few days. These happen because one side grows faster than the other. Keep these two kinds separate in your answers.

slides.heading: Touch-me-not: a quick response
slides.body_md: When a **touch-me-not** (*Mimosa pudica*) leaf is touched, its leaflets fold and droop within seconds. Information passes from cell to cell by **electrical-chemical signals**, and cells at the base of the leaflets **lose water**, change shape, and the leaflets fold.

The plant has no nerves, so the message passes from cell to cell as electrical and chemical changes. Special cells lose water quickly, become limp, and the leaflets close. When water returns, the leaves open again. Notice that the plant does not grow during this movement.

slides.heading: Tropisms: growth towards or away from a stimulus
slides.body_md: A **tropism** is a **directional growth movement** in response to a stimulus. Growth **towards** the stimulus is **positive**; growth **away** is **negative**.

rows: Root grows downwards (positive); shoot grows upwards (negative)
Pollen tube grows towards the ovule

visual.alt: Table of five tropisms with their stimulus and an example of each

slides.narration: Tropism comes from a Greek word meaning turning. Each tropism is named after its stimulus: photo for light, geo for the earth’s gravity, hydro for water, chemo for chemicals and thigmo for touch. If the plant part grows towards the stimulus we call it positive; if it grows away, negative. A shoot is positively phototropic and negatively geotropic. A root is the opposite.

slides.heading: Phototropism and geotropism in action
slides.body_md: Shoots grow **towards light** and **away from gravity**. Roots grow **towards gravity**. Lay a seedling on its side in the dark and both bend within a day or two.

In a day or two, the shoot curves upwards and the root curves downwards, even without light. This shows that gravity alone can direct growth. Both responses help the plant: leaves reach light, and roots reach water and anchorage.

slides.heading: More tropisms: water, chemicals and touch
slides.body_md: Roots grow towards moist soil (**hydrotropism**). A **pollen tube** grows down the style towards the ovule, guided by chemicals (**chemotropism**). **Tendrils** of climbers coil around supports (**thigmotropism**): the side touching the support grows more slowly than the side away from it.

Where a tendril touches the support, it grows slowly, while the outer side keeps growing faster, so the tendril curls around. Underground, roots bend towards moist soil. And inside a flower, the pollen tube follows a chemical trail all the way to the ovule.

slides.narration: Quick check. What guides the pollen tube: light, gravity, water, touch or chemicals? Name the tropism from its stimulus.

slides.body_md: **Auxin** is a plant hormone made at the shoot tip. When light falls from one side, auxin moves to the **shaded side**. There it makes cells **grow longer**, so the shaded side grows more and the shoot **bends towards the light**.

slides.narration: Here is the chemistry behind phototropism. The shoot tip makes a hormone called auxin, which makes cells stretch and grow longer. When light comes from one side, auxin collects on the darker side. Cells there grow longer than cells on the lit side. A shoot that grows more on one side must curve, and it curves towards the light. No muscles, just clever growth.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a seedling experiment
slides.body_md: Three sets of oat seedlings are lit from the right for two days. Explain the results.
bullets: Step 1 — Set A (tip uncovered): bends right. Light from the right moves auxin to the left (shaded) side, which grows more.
Step 2 — Set B (tip covered by a foil cap): grows straight. The tip cannot sense the direction of light, so auxin is spread evenly.
Step 3 — Set C (tip cut off): little growth, no bending. The tip, the source of auxin, is gone.
Conclusion — the **tip** senses light and makes **auxin**; unequal auxin causes **unequal growth**, which is bending.

visual.alt: Worked table of three seedling treatments, their results and the reasons, showing that the tip senses light and makes auxin

slides.narration: This experiment is like a detective story. Each set changes one thing about the tip. When the tip is free, the seedling bends. Cover the tip, and it grows straight. Remove the tip, and growth almost stops. So the tip must both sense light and send a growth signal down the stem. That signal is auxin. In exams, always link the result to the reason.

slides.heading: Plant hormones
slides.body_md: Plant hormones (**phytohormones**) are chemicals made in one part of a plant that coordinate growth and responses in other parts.

rows: Cell elongation at the shoot tip; bending towards light
Inhibits growth; causes wilting of leaves

visual.alt: Table of four plant hormones, their main roles and an example of each

slides.narration: Plants use four main hormones in your syllabus. Auxin makes cells grow longer. Gibberellins help stems grow. Cytokinins encourage cell division, so they are plentiful where cells divide fast, in fruits and seeds. Abscisic acid is the brake: it slows growth and is linked with the wilting of leaves, especially when water is short. Three promote growth; one holds it back.

slides.heading: Quick check: the growth inhibitor
slides.body_md: Which plant hormone inhibits growth and is associated with the wilting of leaves?
slides.narration: Your turn. Three of the four plant hormones promote growth. Which one acts as the brake?

slides.heading: Hormones in animals
slides.body_md: **Hormones** are chemical messengers made by **endocrine glands**. These glands have **no ducts**; they release hormones **directly into the blood**, which carries them to **target cells** that respond.

visual.alt: Flow from an endocrine gland releasing a hormone into the blood to target cells that respond

slides.narration: A hormone is like a letter posted to a particular address. The gland drops it into the bloodstream, which reaches every part of the body. But only cells with the right receptors, the target cells, open the letter and respond. Because endocrine glands have no ducts, they are also called ductless glands. Together they form the endocrine system.

slides.heading: The endocrine glands
slides.body_md: Major endocrine glands: **hypothalamus**, **pituitary**, **pineal**, **thyroid**, **thymus**, **pancreas**, **adrenal glands**, **testes** (males) and **ovaries** (females).

slides.narration: Here is a map of the endocrine glands. In the head are the hypothalamus, the pituitary and the pineal gland. The thyroid sits in the neck like a butterfly. The thymus is in the chest. The pancreas lies in the abdomen, and the adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys like caps. The testes in males and the ovaries in females make the sex hormones.

slides.heading: Glands, hormones and their functions
slides.body_md: Each gland releases particular hormones with particular jobs.

rows: Stimulate the pituitary to release its hormones
Growth and development of the body
Controls the use of carbohydrates, proteins and fats

visual.alt: Table of seven glands with the hormone each makes and its function

slides.narration: This table is worth learning well, because it appears in many questions. Read across each row: gland, hormone, job. A handy trick is to group them. The hypothalamus and pituitary are the control pair in the head. Thyroxine and insulin manage how the body uses food. Adrenaline is for emergencies. Testosterone and oestrogen bring the changes of puberty.

slides.heading: Thyroxine, iodine and goitre
slides.body_md: The thyroid needs **iodine** to make **thyroxine**. Without enough iodine in the diet, the thyroid swells, causing **goitre** (a swollen neck). **Iodised salt** supplies the iodine we need.

nodes.label: Too little iodine in the diet

visual.alt: Flow from low dietary iodine to too little thyroxine, an enlarged thyroid and goitre

slides.narration: Iodine is needed in very small amounts, but it is essential. The thyroid gland uses it to make thyroxine, which controls how your body uses carbohydrates, proteins and fats. In areas where soil and water have little iodine, such as some hilly regions, goitre was once common. Adding iodine to common salt has prevented this for millions of people across India.

slides.heading: Growth hormone and puberty
slides.body_md: **Growth hormone** from the pituitary controls growth. Too little in childhood causes **dwarfism**; too much causes **gigantism**. At **puberty**, **testosterone** (testes) and **oestrogen** (ovaries) bring about the changes of growing up.

rows: Deeper voice, facial hair, muscle growth
Breast development, start of the menstrual cycle

visual.alt: Table of growth hormone and sex hormones with the effects of too little and their roles

slides.narration: Have you noticed how classmates grow at different speeds in Classes nine and ten? That is hormones at work. Growth hormone from the pituitary decides how tall we grow. The sex hormones start the changes of puberty. These changes happen at different ages for different people, and that is perfectly normal. Doctors can treat many hormone problems if they are found early.

slides.heading: Insulin and diabetes
slides.body_md: **Insulin**, made by the **pancreas**, helps cells take up glucose and so **lowers blood sugar**. If too little insulin is made, sugar builds up in the blood: this is **diabetes**. Many patients control it with diet, exercise, medicines or **insulin injections**.

visual.alt: Flow from a meal raising blood sugar to the pancreas releasing insulin, cells taking up glucose and blood sugar returning to normal

slides.narration: After you eat a plate of rice, glucose floods into your blood. The pancreas senses this and releases insulin, which helps body cells take up glucose. Blood sugar comes back to normal. In diabetes, the pancreas does not make enough insulin, so blood sugar stays high and damages the body over time. India has a very large number of people with diabetes, so understanding insulin really matters.

slides.heading: Feedback: keeping hormones in balance
slides.body_md: The **timing and amount** of a hormone are controlled by **feedback**. When blood sugar rises, the pancreas releases more insulin; as sugar falls back to normal, insulin release is **reduced**.

visual.alt: Feedback loop: high blood sugar causes more insulin, sugar falls to normal, insulin release drops, until sugar rises again

slides.narration: Think of a ceiling fan with a regulator that adjusts itself. When the room heats up, the fan speeds up; when it cools, the fan slows down. Hormones work the same way. The result of a hormone feeds back to the gland and changes how much it releases. This feedback keeps the level just right, never too high and never too low.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading a blood sugar graph
slides.body_md: The graph shows blood glucose after the same meal for two people. Interpret it.
bullets: Step 1 — Healthy person: rises from 90 to 140 at 30 minutes, back to 90 by 150 minutes.
Step 2 — Explanation: rising sugar triggers insulin; insulin lowers sugar; as sugar falls, less insulin is released (feedback).
Step 3 — Second person: starts high (150), peaks near 260 and is still above 200 after 150 minutes.
Conclusion — too little insulin (or cells not responding to it): signs of **diabetes**; a doctor would confirm with further tests.

visual.alt: Line graph of blood glucose after a meal: the healthy person rises from 90 to 140 and returns to 90 within two and a half hours; the person with untreated diabetes starts at 150, rises to about 260 and is still above 200 at 150 minutes
visual.caption: Typical values for illustration, not a medical reference.

slides.narration: Graphs like this often appear in case-based questions. Read the starting value, the peak and the time to return. For the healthy person, sugar rises after the meal but comes back down within two and a half hours, thanks to insulin and feedback. For the second person, sugar stays high, which suggests the body is not making or using enough insulin. Always describe, then explain.

slides.heading: Quick check: why feedback?
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about feedback control of hormones.
slides.narration: Quick check. Read both statements carefully. Is each true on its own? Then ask whether the reason really explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Nervous and hormonal coordination compared
slides.body_md: Both systems coordinate the body, but in different ways.
columns:
**Nervous system**

- Electrical impulses along nerves
- Very fast; effect is short
- Reaches only cells connected by nerves
- Example: reflex action

**Endocrine system**

- Chemical messengers in the blood
- Slower; effect lasts longer
- Reaches all cells; only target cells respond
- Example: growth, puberty, blood sugar

visual.alt: Table comparing nervous and hormonal coordination by message, carrier, speed and duration

slides.narration: Here is the big picture. The nervous system is the body’s express service: quick, precise and short-lived. The endocrine system is the slow, steady postal service: it reaches everywhere and its effects last. They often work together. When you are frightened, nerves make you jump at once, and adrenaline keeps your heart racing for several minutes afterwards.

slides.heading: Summary: plants and hormones
bullets: Touch-me-not: immediate movement by water loss from cells, no growth.
Tropisms are directional growth movements: photo-, geo-, hydro-, chemo- and thigmotropism.
Auxin moves to the shaded side, cells there grow longer, and the shoot bends towards light.
Auxin and gibberellins promote growth, cytokinins promote cell division, abscisic acid inhibits growth.
Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood; feedback controls the amount and timing.
Iodine → thyroxine (goitre if lacking); insulin lowers blood sugar (diabetes if lacking).

visual.alt: Summary table of five hormones with their source and one key fact

slides.narration: Let us wrap up. Plants move quickly by changing the water in their cells, or slowly by growing unequally, guided by auxin and other hormones. Animals add a hormonal system to their nerves. Endocrine glands post their chemical messages into the blood, and feedback keeps the levels right. Remember the two classic deficiency stories: no iodine causes goitre, and too little insulin causes diabetes.

slides.heading: Exam tips: plants and hormones
bullets: Do not call the touch-me-not response a tropism; it is not a growth movement and not directional.
Write "positive" or "negative" with each tropism, e.g. roots are **positively geotropic**.
For phototropism, mention all three: auxin made at the tip, moves to the shaded side, cells there elongate.
Spell and match carefully: thyroxine–thyroid, insulin–pancreas, adrenaline–adrenal.
Feedback answers need both directions: more hormone when the level is high, less when it returns to normal.
Typical 3-mark split: name (1) + mechanism (1) + example or effect (1).

rows: Shoot bends because light pushes it
Unequal growth caused by auxin on the shaded side
Hormones go only to their target organ
Hormones reach all cells; only target cells respond
Goitre is caused by too much iodine
Goitre is caused by too little iodine

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes about plant movements and hormones with the correct ideas

slides.narration: Here is how to avoid the usual traps. Never say light pushes or pulls a shoot; growth does the bending. Give the full auxin story in three steps. When writing about hormones, always pair the gland with its hormone and its job. And in feedback questions, describe both halves of the loop. Examiners reward precise words like elongation, target cells and ductless.

notes.title: Control and Coordination — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Why coordination? Receptors, neurons and synapses
sections.body_md:
A **stimulus** is a change in the surroundings (light, heat, sound, touch, chemicals). Organisms respond to stimuli in a controlled way; **control and coordination** make the right parts act together, at the right time and in the right amount. In animals this is done by the **nervous system** and the **endocrine (hormonal) system**.

**Receptors** are specialised cells, usually in sense organs, that detect stimuli: photoreceptors (eye), phonoreceptors (ear), olfactory receptors (nose), gustatory receptors (tongue), and touch, heat and pain receptors (skin). **Effectors** are the muscles and glands that respond.

A **neuron** is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system: **dendrites** acquire information → **cell body** (with nucleus) → **axon** carries the **electrical impulse** → **nerve endings**. At the nerve ending the impulse causes the release of **chemicals**, which cross a small gap, the **synapse**, and start a new electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron. A similar junction passes impulses to muscles and glands. Because chemicals are released only at the axon end, impulses cross a synapse in **one direction only**.

key_terms.definition_md: A change in the environment to which an organism responds.
A cell or group of cells that detects a particular stimulus.
A muscle or gland that carries out the response.
The gap between the nerve ending of one neuron and the dendrite of the next, crossed by chemicals.

sections.heading: 2. Reflex action and the reflex arc
sections.body_md:
Actions are **voluntary** (by choice, controlled by the forebrain, e.g. writing), **involuntary** (automatic, controlled by the midbrain and hindbrain, e.g. heartbeat, salivation) or **reflex** (a sudden, automatic response to a stimulus without conscious thought, e.g. pulling the hand away from a flame).

The path of a reflex is the **reflex arc**: **receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → effector**. Reflex arcs are formed in the **spinal cord**, close to where the nerves enter, so the response is very quick and protects the body. The impulse also travels to the brain, which becomes aware of the event after the response has begun — that is why pain is felt a moment after the hand moves.

Reflex arcs are thought to have evolved because they are efficient where real thinking is not fast enough; the brain still handles the complex decisions.

key_terms.definition_md: A sudden, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus.
The pathway of a reflex: receptor, sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron, effector.
A neuron in the spinal cord connecting the sensory neuron to the motor neuron.

sections.heading: 3. The human brain
sections.body_md:
The **central nervous system (CNS)** is the brain and the spinal cord; the **peripheral nervous system (PNS)** is the **cranial nerves** (from the brain) and **spinal nerves** (from the spinal cord).

- **Forebrain (cerebrum):** the main thinking part. Sensory areas receive impulses (sight, hearing, smell, touch); association areas link them with memory; motor areas control **voluntary** muscles.
- **Midbrain:** some involuntary actions, including reflex movements of the head and eyes.
- **Hindbrain:** **medulla** — blood pressure, salivation and vomiting; **pons** — helps regulate breathing; **cerebellum** — posture, balance and the precision of voluntary actions (walking straight, riding a bicycle, picking up a pencil).

key_terms.definition_md: The large forebrain; thinking, memory, senses and voluntary actions.
Part of the hindbrain that maintains posture and balance and makes movements precise.
Part of the hindbrain that controls blood pressure, salivation and vomiting.

sections.heading: 4. Protection, movement and the limits of nerve impulses
sections.body_md:
The brain lies in a bony box, the **skull (cranium)**, and is cushioned by **fluid** that absorbs shocks. The spinal cord is protected by the **vertebral column**.

When an impulse reaches a muscle, special **proteins** in the muscle cells change their shape and arrangement, the cells **shorten**, and the part moves.

Electrical impulses have limits: they reach **only cells connected by nervous tissue**, and a cell needs time to **reset** after each impulse before it can send another. So multicellular organisms also use **chemical communication** — hormones carried by the blood, which reach all cells (only cells with the right receptors respond). Plants, which have no nervous tissue, rely on chemical and electrical-chemical signals.

key_terms.definition_md: The backbone, which encloses and protects the spinal cord.

sections.heading: 5. Movements in plants
sections.body_md:
Plants have no nervous system, yet they respond to stimuli in two ways.

**Immediate response (no growth):** the leaflets of the **touch-me-not** (*Mimosa pudica*) fold and droop within seconds of a touch. Information passes from cell to cell by electrical-chemical means, and certain cells change shape by **losing water**. The movement is not directional and involves no growth (a nastic movement).

**Growth movements (tropisms):** directional growth towards (positive) or away from (negative) a stimulus, caused by unequal growth on two sides:
- **Phototropism** — shoots grow towards light; roots away from it.
- **Geotropism** — roots grow towards gravity (positive); shoots away (negative).
- **Hydrotropism** — roots grow towards water.
- **Chemotropism** — the pollen tube grows towards the ovule.
- **Thigmotropism** — tendrils coil around a support because the side touching it grows more slowly than the side away from it.

key_terms.definition_md: A directional growth movement of a plant part in response to a stimulus.
Growth towards the stimulus, e.g. roots towards gravity.
A non-directional response, e.g. folding of touch-me-not leaflets.

sections.heading: 6. Plant hormones
sections.body_md:
Plant hormones (phytohormones) coordinate growth and responses.

- **Auxin** — made at the shoot tip; makes cells **elongate**. When light comes from one side, auxin diffuses to the **shaded side**, cells there grow longer, and the shoot bends towards the light.
- **Gibberellins** — help the **growth of the stem**.
- **Cytokinins** — promote **cell division**; found in high concentration where cells divide rapidly, such as fruits and seeds.
- **Abscisic acid** — **inhibits growth**; its effects include the **wilting of leaves**; it is linked with responses to water stress.

key_terms.definition_md: Plant hormone made at the shoot tip that causes cell elongation.
Plant hormone that inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves.

sections.heading: 7. Hormones in animals and feedback
sections.body_md:
**Endocrine glands** are ductless: they release **hormones** directly into the blood, which carries them to **target cells**.

| Gland | Hormone | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Hypothalamus | Releasing hormones | Stimulate the pituitary |
| Pituitary | Growth hormone | Growth and development; deficiency in childhood causes dwarfism |
| Thyroid | Thyroxine | Controls carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism; needs **iodine** |
| Pancreas | Insulin | Lowers blood sugar; deficiency causes **diabetes** |
| Adrenal | Adrenaline | Prepares the body for emergencies |
| Testes | Testosterone | Changes in males at puberty |
| Ovaries | Oestrogen | Changes in females at puberty |

**Adrenaline** is released into the blood in an emergency: the heart beats faster, sending more oxygen to the muscles; blood supply to the digestive system and skin is reduced as small arteries there contract; breathing becomes faster. **Iodised salt** prevents iodine deficiency and **goitre** (swollen neck).

**Feedback mechanism:** the timing and amount of hormone release are regulated by feedback. For example, when blood sugar rises, cells of the pancreas detect it and release more insulin; as the level falls, insulin secretion is reduced.

key_terms.definition_md: A ductless gland that releases hormones directly into the blood.
A chemical messenger made in one place and acting on target cells elsewhere.
Control in which the effect of a hormone regulates further release of that hormone.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing the impulse direction backwards (it is dendrite → cell body → axon → nerve ending).
- Calling the synapse a physical joint; it is a gap crossed by chemicals, in one direction only.
- Saying reflexes are controlled by the brain; the reflex arc is in the spinal cord (the brain is informed afterwards).
- Mixing up cerebrum (thinking) and cerebellum (balance).
- Calling the touch-me-not response a tropism; it is an immediate, non-growth, non-directional movement.
- Saying light "pulls" the shoot; bending is due to unequal growth caused by auxin.
- Writing that insulin raises blood sugar, or that goitre is caused by too much iodine.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: correct option, term or matching pair.
- 2–3-mark answers: correct term (1) + mechanism or pathway (1) + example or reason (1).
- 5-mark answers: labelled diagram (neuron, reflex arc or brain) (2) + explanation in the correct order (2) + one extra point such as significance or a comparison (1).
- Case-based items: two 1-mark parts from the passage and a 2-mark part with an internal choice, often interpreting data.

cards.back_md: A change in the surroundings (light, heat, sound, touch, chemicals) to which an organism responds.

cards.front_md: Name the receptors for taste and smell.
cards.back_md: Gustatory receptors (taste buds of the tongue) and olfactory receptors (nose).

cards.front_md: Order in which an impulse travels through a neuron?
cards.back_md: Dendrite → cell body → axon → nerve ending.
The gap between the nerve ending of one neuron and the dendrite of the next; chemicals released at the nerve ending cross it.

cards.front_md: Why does an impulse cross a synapse in one direction only?
cards.back_md: Chemicals are released only at the axon ending and are received by the dendrite of the next neuron.
Muscles and glands that carry out a response.
A sudden, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, without conscious thinking.

cards.front_md: Parts of a reflex arc, in order?
cards.back_md: Receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron (spinal cord) → motor neuron → effector.
In the spinal cord.

cards.front_md: Why do you feel pain only after pulling your hand away?
cards.back_md: The reflex response is made by the spinal cord; the message reaches the brain slightly later.

cards.front_md: Give one voluntary, one involuntary and one reflex action.
cards.back_md: Writing (voluntary); heartbeat (involuntary); withdrawing the hand from a flame (reflex).

cards.front_md: What makes up the central nervous system?
cards.back_md: The brain and the spinal cord.

cards.front_md: Cranial nerves and spinal nerves arise from…?
cards.back_md: Cranial nerves from the brain; spinal nerves from the spinal cord. Together they form the peripheral nervous system.
Controls blood pressure, salivation and vomiting.
Maintains posture and balance; makes voluntary movements precise.

cards.front_md: Which part of the brain controls thinking and voluntary actions?
cards.back_md: The forebrain (cerebrum).
By the bony skull (cranium) and a cushion of fluid that absorbs shocks.

cards.front_md: How does a muscle cell move?
cards.back_md: Special proteins change their shape and arrangement, so the cell shortens.
They reach only cells connected by nerves, and cells need time to reset before the next impulse.
Electrical-chemical signals pass between cells; cells lose water and change shape. No growth is involved.
A directional growth movement of a plant part in response to a stimulus.
Roots are positively geotropic (grow down); shoots are negatively geotropic (grow up).

cards.front_md: Pollen tube growing towards the ovule is…?
cards.back_md: Chemotropism.

cards.front_md: Why does a tendril coil around a stick?
cards.back_md: The side touching the stick grows more slowly than the side away from it (thigmotropism).

cards.front_md: How does auxin cause a shoot to bend towards light?
cards.back_md: Auxin moves to the shaded side; cells there elongate more, so the shoot curves towards the light.
Gibberellins: stem growth. Cytokinins: promote cell division (high in fruits and seeds).
Abscisic acid (also causes wilting of leaves).
Ductless glands that release hormones directly into the blood.
Iodine is needed to make thyroxine; lack of it causes goitre.
Pancreas; lowers blood sugar. Too little causes diabetes.
Faster heartbeat and breathing; more blood to muscles, less to the gut and skin — ready for an emergency.
Control in which the level of a substance regulates hormone release: high blood sugar → more insulin; normal sugar → less insulin.
Touch-me-not folding is not a growth movement and not directional — do not call it a tropism.

questions.stem_md: In which order does a nerve impulse travel through a neuron?

options.text_md: Axon → cell body → dendrite → nerve ending
Cell body → dendrite → axon → nerve ending
Nerve ending → axon → cell body → dendrite
Dendrite → cell body → axon → nerve ending

questions.solution_md: Information is picked up at the tips of the dendrites, passes through the cell body, travels along the axon and leaves at the nerve ending — option (d). The other orders start at the wrong end or skip the cell body.

questions.stem_md: The axon ending of neuron **P** lies next to a dendrite of neuron **Q**, separated by a synapse. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: A message can pass from Q to P, but not from P to Q.
A message can pass from P to Q, but not from Q to P.
Messages pass equally well in both directions.
No message can pass, because the two neurons do not touch.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Chemicals are released only at an axon ending and act on a dendrite.

Step 2 — P has the axon ending and Q has the dendrite, so the message goes from P to Q only — option (b).

Step 3 — (a) reverses the direction; (c) ignores the one-way release of chemicals; (d) forgets that chemicals carry the message across the gap.

questions.stem_md: How does a nerve message cross a synapse?

options.text_md: Chemicals released at the nerve ending cross the gap and start a new impulse in the next neuron.
The electrical impulse jumps directly across the gap.
Blood carries the message from one neuron to the next.
The two neurons join together for a moment so that the impulse can pass.

questions.solution_md: At the end of the axon, the electrical impulse sets off the release of chemicals. They cross the synapse and start a new electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron — option (a). The impulse cannot jump the gap (b), blood is not involved (c), and neurons do not join (d).

questions.stem_md: Ritu has a heavy cold with a blocked nose. At a perfume shop she cannot smell the scent sprayed on her wrist, yet she clearly feels that the spray is cool and wet. Which receptors are not being stimulated?

options.text_md: Olfactory receptors in the nose
Touch and cold receptors in the skin
Gustatory receptors in the tongue
Photoreceptors in the eye

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — She feels the cool, wet spray, so the touch and cold receptors in her skin (b) are working.

Step 2 — Smell is detected by olfactory receptors in the nose; the blocked nose stops the scent from reaching them — option (a).

Step 3 — Taste (c) and sight (d) have nothing to do with smelling the perfume.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an **effector**?

options.text_md: The taste bud that detects sweetness
The spinal cord that connects sensory and motor neurons
The salivary gland that releases saliva when food is smelt
The sensory nerve from the skin of the hand

questions.solution_md: Effectors are muscles and glands that carry out a response. The salivary gland responds by releasing saliva — option (c). A taste bud is a receptor (a), the spinal cord is part of the central nervous system (b), and a sensory nerve only carries impulses to it (d).

questions.stem_md: A poison stops the release of chemicals at every nerve ending in the body. Which effect would you expect?

options.text_md: Only voluntary actions would stop; reflexes would continue because they do not use the brain.
Only hormones would stop working; nerve messages would be unaffected.
Nerve messages would travel faster because there would be no delay at synapses.
Messages could not pass from neuron to neuron or to muscles, so both reflexes and voluntary movements would fail.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Every nerve pathway, including a reflex arc, passes messages across synapses and to muscles using chemicals.

Step 2 — With no chemicals released, no message can reach the next neuron or the muscle, so all nerve-controlled responses fail — option (d).

Step 3 — (a) is wrong because reflex arcs also have synapses; (b) confuses nerves with hormones; (c) is wrong because without chemicals the message does not cross at all.

questions.stem_md: In an accident, the **sensory** nerves from Aarav’s right hand are damaged, but the **motor** nerves are unharmed. What is most likely?

options.text_md: He can feel a pin prick on the hand but cannot move it.
He can move the hand when he decides to, but cannot feel a pin prick on it.
He can neither feel nor move the hand.
He can feel and move the hand normally; only his reflexes are lost.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Sensory nerves carry impulses from receptors to the brain and spinal cord; without them, touch and pain from the hand cannot be felt.

Step 2 — Motor nerves carry instructions to the muscles; these work, so he can still move the hand voluntarily — option (b).

Step 3 — (a) swaps the roles of the two nerves; (c) needs both kinds of nerve damaged; (d) is wrong because feeling depends on the sensory nerves.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A nerve impulse crosses a synapse in only one direction.

**Reason (R):** Chemicals are released only at the axon ending of one neuron and act on the dendrite of the next neuron.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Because the chemicals are released only from the axon ending and received by the next dendrite, the message can only go one way. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the part of a neuron where information is first picked up, and the part along which it travels as an electrical impulse.

(b) What happens at the end of the axon so that the message reaches the next neuron?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Information is picked up at the tips of the **dendrites**, and it travels as an electrical impulse along the **axon**.

(b) The impulse sets off the release of **chemicals** at the nerve ending. These cross the **synapse** and start a new electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Recall the direction of travel: dendrite → cell body → axon → nerve ending.

Step 2 — At the nerve ending the electrical signal becomes a chemical one, which crosses the gap.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Chemicals released, cross the synapse and start a new impulse

questions.stem_md:
Kiran argues: "Nerve impulses are the fastest messages in the body, so the body should use nerves for every kind of control, including growth." Evaluate his claim by answering the following.

(a) State two limitations of electrical impulses.

(b) How do hormones overcome these limitations?

(c) Why can plants coordinate their growth using chemicals alone?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Impulses reach only cells connected by nervous tissue, and a cell needs time to reset after each impulse, so it cannot send impulses continuously.

(b) Hormones travel in the blood to every cell, and their effect lasts long — exactly what slow, body-wide jobs such as growth need.

(c) Plants have no nervous tissue, and growth is slow, so chemicals moving from cell to cell are enough.

So Kiran is wrong: speed is not the only need.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Recall the two limits: reach (only connected cells) and the reset time.

Step 2 — Hormones travel in the blood to all cells and act for long periods.

Step 3 — Plants lack nerves and their growth responses are slow, so the claim fails.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Hormones reach all cells through the blood and act for long
(c) No nervous tissue; slow responses suit chemical signals

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a neuron and mark the direction in which the impulse travels.

(b) Describe how information picked up by a receptor is passed from one neuron to the next.

(c) Explain why the message travels in one direction only.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Diagram with labels: **dendrites**, **cell body**, **nucleus**, **axon**, **nerve endings**; an arrow from the dendrites towards the nerve endings.

(b) A stimulus at the dendrite tip sets off a chemical reaction that produces an **electrical impulse**. The impulse travels from the dendrite to the cell body and along the axon to the nerve ending. There it causes the release of **chemicals**, which cross the **synapse** and start a similar electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron. In this way the message is relayed until it reaches the brain or spinal cord, or a muscle or gland.

(c) The chemicals are released only from the axon ending and are received only by the dendrite of the next neuron, so the message cannot travel backwards.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Draw and label the five parts, with the direction arrow.

Step 2 — Describe the electrical part (inside the neuron) and the chemical part (across the synapse).

Step 3 — Link one-way travel to where the chemicals are released.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Neat diagram with at least four correct labels
(a) Arrow showing the direction of the impulse
(b) Electrical impulse from dendrite through cell body and axon
(b) Chemicals cross the synapse and start a new impulse
(c) One-way release and reception of chemicals

questions.stem_md:
An infection damages Rahul’s facial nerve, a nerve that arises from the brain and supplies the muscles of the face. One side of his face cannot smile, but he moves his arms normally.

(a) Is the facial nerve part of the central or the peripheral nervous system? Give a reason.

(b) Why are his arm movements unaffected?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **peripheral** nervous system. It is a **cranial nerve**: it arises from the brain and connects it to the face muscles; the central nervous system is only the brain and spinal cord.

(b) His arm muscles receive instructions through **spinal nerves** from the spinal cord, which are not damaged.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Nerves arising from the brain are cranial nerves, part of the peripheral system.

Step 2 — The arms are served by a different route: spinal nerves.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Peripheral, because it is a cranial nerve linking the brain to the face
(b) Arms are supplied by undamaged spinal nerves

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a reflex action?

options.text_md: Writing your name on an answer sheet
Pulling your foot back suddenly on stepping on a sharp stone
Choosing ripe bananas at a fruit stall
Kicking a football towards the goal

questions.solution_md: A reflex is a sudden, automatic response to a stimulus, made without thinking. Pulling the foot off a sharp stone fits — option (b). The other three are voluntary actions that need thought and choice.

questions.stem_md: In a reflex such as pulling your foot off a sharp stone, where is the sensory neuron connected to the motor neuron?

options.text_md: In the cerebellum
In the forebrain
In the muscle of the leg
In the spinal cord

questions.solution_md: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord, where a relay neuron connects the sensory neuron to the motor neuron — option (d). The brain is informed but does not make this connection (a, b); the leg muscle is the effector (c).

questions.stem_md: Gita steps on a nail. She feels the sharp pain at once, but her foot does not pull away, and she also finds she cannot move that leg when she tries to. Which part of the pathway is most likely damaged?

options.text_md: The sensory neuron from the foot
The pain receptors in the skin of the foot
The motor neuron to the leg muscles
The forebrain, where pain is felt

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — She feels the pain, so the receptors (b), the sensory neuron (a) and the route to the forebrain (d) are all working.

Step 2 — Neither the reflex nor her own decision can move the leg. Both use the motor neuron to reach the muscle, so the motor neuron is the likely damaged part — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Four things happen to Lakshmi one morning. Which one is a reflex action produced by the spinal cord?

options.text_md: Her heart beats faster as she climbs the stairs.
She decides to drink water because she feels thirsty.
She jerks her hand back when it brushes against a hot iron.
She keeps her balance while standing in a moving bus.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Jerking the hand from a hot iron is sudden, automatic and protective: a spinal reflex — option (c).

Step 2 — A faster heartbeat (a) is an involuntary action controlled by the hindbrain; deciding to drink (b) is a voluntary action of the forebrain; balance (d) is maintained by the cerebellum.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A reflex action takes less time than an action that needs thinking.

**Reason (R):** In a reflex action, the impulse first goes to the brain, which decides the response.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the reflex path is short. R is false: the reflex arc is completed in the spinal cord, and the brain is informed only afterwards — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a reflex action, information about the stimulus never reaches the brain.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The reflex response is produced by the spinal cord, but the message also travels up to the brain, which becomes aware of it a moment later.

questions.stem_md: A withdrawal reflex sends an impulse $0.9\ \text{m}$ from a fingertip to the spinal cord and $0.9\ \text{m}$ back to the arm muscles. If impulses in these neurons travel at $60\ \text{m/s}$, how long, in **milliseconds**, does the conduction take? (Ignore delays at synapses.)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Total distance $= 0.9 + 0.9 = 1.8\ \text{m}$.

Step 2 — Time $= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} = \dfrac{1.8}{60} = 0.03\ \text{s}$.

Step 3 — In milliseconds: $0.03 \times 1000 = 30\ \text{ms}$.

questions.stem_md: Kabir accidentally touches a hot iron and jerks his hand away. Only a moment later does he feel the pain. Explain both observations.

answer.model_answer_md: Pulling the hand away is a **reflex action**: impulses from heat receptors travel along a sensory neuron to the **spinal cord**, where a relay neuron passes them to a motor neuron, and the arm muscle contracts. The message reaches the **brain** later, by a longer path, so the pain is felt after the hand has moved.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Identify the reflex arc through the spinal cord.

Step 2 — Explain the delay: the brain receives the message later.

marking_scheme.step: Reflex arc through the spinal cord gives the quick withdrawal
Message reaches the brain later, so the pain is felt afterwards

questions.stem_md:
Meenakshi’s spinal cord was injured in the middle of her back. When a doctor pricks her toe with a pin, her leg pulls away, but she says she felt nothing.

(a) Which part of her nervous system produced the leg movement? Explain.

(b) Why did she feel nothing?

(c) She can still feel a pin prick on her hand. Why?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A **reflex arc** in the spinal cord **below** the injury: receptor in the toe → sensory neuron → relay neuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → leg muscle. The brain is not needed for this response.

(b) To be felt, the impulse must travel up the spinal cord to the brain; the injury blocks this path, so the brain never receives the message.

(c) Nerves from the hand join the spinal cord **above** the injury, so their impulses can still reach the brain.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Movement without feeling means a reflex that does not need the brain.

Step 2 — Feeling needs the message to reach the brain; the injury cuts that route.

Step 3 — Compare where the nerves from the hand and from the foot join the spinal cord.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Reflex arc in the spinal cord below the injury
(b) The route up to the brain is blocked
(c) Hand nerves join the cord above the injury

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is a reflex action? Give two examples.

(b) Draw a labelled diagram of a reflex arc.

(c) Why are reflex arcs completed in the spinal cord, even though the brain is the main thinking centre?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A reflex action is a sudden, automatic response to a stimulus, made without conscious thinking. Examples: pulling the hand away from a candle flame; pulling the foot off a sharp thorn.

(b) Diagram labels: **receptor** (in the skin), **sensory neuron**, **spinal cord** with **relay neuron**, **motor neuron**, **effector** (muscle), with arrows showing the direction of the impulse.

(c) Thinking takes time, and in danger there is no time to waste. Because the sensory and motor neurons are connected in the spinal cord, close to where the nerves enter, the message travels a short path and the response is very quick, protecting the body. The brain is still informed, so it can decide what to do next.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Define a reflex and give two protective examples.

Step 2 — Draw the five parts of the arc with arrows.

Step 3 — Explain the benefit of the short path.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Short path gives a quick protective response; brain informed later

questions.stem_md: Match each action in Column A with the part of the nervous system that mainly controls it in Column B.

options.text_md: Pulling the hand away from a flame
Keeping blood pressure steady
Writing an essay
Riding a bicycle without wobbling

questions.solution_md: A reflex is controlled by the spinal cord (1 → r); blood pressure by the medulla (2 → p); thinking and writing by the forebrain (3 → s); balance and precise movement by the cerebellum (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: After a head injury, a cyclist can think and speak clearly but cannot keep his balance or pick up a pen precisely. Which part of the brain is most likely affected?

options.text_md: Medulla
Forebrain (cerebrum)
Pituitary gland
Cerebellum

questions.solution_md: Balance and precise movement are controlled by the cerebellum — option (d). His thinking is normal, which rules out the forebrain (b); the medulla (a) controls blood pressure, salivation and vomiting; the pituitary (c) is a gland, not a control centre for movement.

questions.stem_md: Blood pressure, salivation and vomiting are controlled by the:

options.text_md: cerebellum
medulla
cerebrum
pituitary gland

questions.solution_md: These involuntary actions are controlled by the medulla in the hindbrain — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The central nervous system consists of:

options.text_md: the brain and the cranial nerves
the brain and the spinal cord
the spinal cord and the spinal nerves
all the nerves of the body

questions.solution_md: The central nervous system is the brain and the spinal cord — option (b). Cranial and spinal nerves belong to the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem_md: Asha hears someone call her name, recognises her friend’s voice and decides to turn and wave. Which part of the brain links the sound with her memory and makes the decision?

options.text_md: Cerebellum
Medulla
Forebrain
Spinal cord

questions.solution_md: Recognising a voice, using memory and deciding to act are jobs of the forebrain (cerebrum) — option (c). The cerebellum makes the wave smooth but does not decide; the medulla controls involuntary actions; the spinal cord handles reflexes.

questions.stem_md: After a bad fall from a tree, a farm worker complains of severe pain in his back. First-aid trainers say he must not be lifted in a way that bends his back. Why?

options.text_md: Bending a broken backbone could crush the spinal cord inside it and cut the link between the brain and the body.
Bending the back would drain the fluid that cushions the brain.
Bending the back would stop the cerebellum from controlling balance.
Bending the back would stop the release of adrenaline.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — The spinal cord runs inside the vertebral column, which protects it.

Step 2 — If the backbone is broken, bending it can crush the cord; messages between the brain and the body below the injury could then be cut, causing loss of feeling and movement — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The cerebellum controls all the involuntary actions of the body.

**Reason (R):** Blood pressure and salivation are controlled by the medulla.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md: Nerves arising from the brain are called ___ nerves, and those arising from the spinal cord are called ___ nerves.

questions.stem_md: How are (a) the brain and (b) the spinal cord protected in the human body?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The brain is enclosed in a bony box, the **skull (cranium)**. Inside it, the brain is surrounded by a **fluid-filled** cushion that absorbs shocks.

questions.solution_md: Name the bony protection of each organ, and the shock-absorbing fluid around the brain.

questions.stem_md:

(b) A patient’s blood pressure stays steady while he sleeps.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.solution_md:

(a) Draw a labelled diagram of the human brain showing the forebrain, midbrain, cerebellum, pons and medulla.

(b) State one function each of the forebrain, the cerebellum and the medulla.

(c) How does an impulse arriving along a motor neuron make a muscle move?

answer.model_answer_md:

(c) Muscle proteins change shape and arrangement
(c) Muscle cells shorten and the part moves

questions.stem_md: The leaflets of a touch-me-not plant fold within seconds of being touched. This happens because:

options.text_md: the leaflets grow rapidly towards the touch
muscle cells in the leaf contract
cells at the base of the leaflets lose water and change shape
auxin collects on the side that is touched

questions.solution_md: The response is too quick to involve growth. Electrical-chemical signals pass between cells, and certain cells lose water and change shape, so the leaflets fold — option (c). Plants have no muscles (b), growth is far slower (a), and auxin acts on growth, not on this quick movement (d).

questions.stem_md: The downward growth of roots in response to gravity is called:

options.text_md: negative geotropism
positive geotropism
positive phototropism
hydrotropism

questions.solution_md: Growth towards the pull of gravity is positive geotropism — option (b). Shoots, which grow upwards, show negative geotropism.

questions.stem_md: Rani lays a germinating bean seedling on its side inside a dark cupboard. What will she see after two days?

options.text_md: Both the shoot and the root curve downwards.
The shoot curves upwards and the root curves downwards.
The shoot curves downwards and the root curves upwards.
Neither changes direction, because there is no light.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Gravity acts even in the dark, so geotropism still works.

Step 2 — The shoot is negatively geotropic (curves up) and the root positively geotropic (curves down) — option (b).

Step 3 — (d) wrongly assumes that light is needed for every tropism.

questions.stem_md: Seedlings in a box with one hole on the right side bend towards the right. If the same box is kept slowly rotating on a turntable, so that the hole faces every direction in turn, the seedlings will most likely:

options.text_md: grow nearly straight up, because each side receives light equally over time
bend even more strongly to the right
bend to the left, away from the hole
stop growing, because the light keeps changing direction

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Bending happens when one side is shaded for long enough for auxin to build up there.

Step 2 — On a slowly turning box, every side is lit and shaded in turn, so growth evens out and the shoots grow nearly straight — option (a).

Step 3 — (b) and (c) assume light from one fixed side; (d) is wrong because light still reaches the shoots.

questions.stem_md: Near a leaking water pipe in a garden, the roots of a neem tree are found growing sideways towards the pipe. This is an example of:

options.text_md: positive hydrotropism
positive geotropism
negative phototropism
chemotropism

questions.solution_md: The roots are growing towards a source of water, so this is positive hydrotropism — option (a). Geotropism (b) would be straight down; light (c) and chemicals (d) are not the stimulus here.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The tendrils of a pea plant coil around a support.

**Reason (R):** The shoot of a plant grows towards light.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between the folding of touch-me-not leaflets when touched and the bending of a shoot towards light.

answer.model_answer_md: Touch-me-not folding is **quick** (seconds) and involves **no growth**: cells lose water and change shape, whatever the direction of the touch. questions.stem_md:
A bitter gourd vine is planted next to a bamboo pole. After a week, its tendrils are wound tightly around the pole.

(a) Name this response.

(b) Explain how the coiling happens.

(c) How does this response help the plant?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Thigmotropism** — a growth response to touch.

(b) The part of the tendril touching the pole grows more slowly than the part away from it. The outer side becomes longer, so the tendril curls around the pole.

(c) The vine has a weak stem. By climbing the pole it lifts its leaves up into the sunlight for photosynthesis without having to build a thick, strong stem.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — The stimulus is touch, so the response is thigmotropism.

Step 2 — Unequal growth on the two sides of the tendril causes coiling.

(c) Climbing helps the leaves reach sunlight

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is a tropism? How is it different from the folding of touch-me-not leaves?

(b) Design a simple experiment, using a seedling in a pot, a cardboard box and a lamp, to show that a shoot is positively phototropic. State what you would observe.

(c) Explain the role of auxin in the result.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A tropism is a **directional growth movement** of a plant part in response to a stimulus. Touch-me-not folding is quick, involves **no growth** and does not depend on the direction of the stimulus.

(b) Water a potted seedling and place it inside a cardboard box with a single hole cut in one side. Keep a lamp shining through the hole, and keep a second seedling in an identical box lit evenly from above as a control. After three to four days, the shoot in the first box bends towards the hole, while the control grows straight up.

(c) Auxin, made at the shoot tip, moves to the **shaded side**. Cells there **grow longer** than on the lit side, so the shoot curves towards the light.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Define tropism and contrast it with a non-growth movement.

Step 2 — Light from one side only, a control, and the observation.

Step 3 — Auxin, shaded side, cell elongation, bending.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Set-up with one-sided light and a control
(b) Observation: shoot bends towards the light
(c) Auxin moves to the shaded side, cells there elongate, shoot bends

questions.stem_md: Which plant hormone inhibits growth and is associated with the wilting of leaves?

options.text_md: Abscisic acid
Auxin
Gibberellin
Cytokinin

questions.stem_md: A plant tissue-culture laboratory in Bengaluru wants a small piece of leaf tissue to divide rapidly and form a mass of new cells. Which plant hormone is most useful for this?

options.text_md: Cytokinin
Abscisic acid
Gibberellin
Oestrogen

questions.stem_md: A sugarcane farmer in Maharashtra wants the stems of his crop to grow taller. Which plant hormone would help most?

Cytokinin
Adrenaline
Gibberellin

questions.solution_md: Gibberellins help the growth of the stem — option (d). Abscisic acid inhibits growth (a); cytokinins mainly promote cell division (b); adrenaline is an animal hormone (c).

On the west side; the shoot bends towards the west.
Evenly on both sides; the shoot grows straight.
On the west side; the shoot bends towards the east.

Step 1 — Auxin moves to the shaded side, which here is the west side.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A shoot lit from one side bends towards the light.

**Reason (R):** Auxin diffuses towards the shaded side of the shoot and makes the cells there grow longer.

questions.stem_md: The plant hormone that promotes cell division is ___.
questions.solution_md: **Cytokinin** promotes cell division.

questions.stem_md: Match each plant hormone in Column A with its main role in Column B.

options.text_md: Auxin
Gibberellin
Cytokinin
Abscisic acid

questions.stem_md: During a long dry spell, the leaves of a mango sapling droop and its growth almost stops. Name the plant hormone mainly involved, and explain how its action can help the sapling survive the dry spell.

answer.model_answer_md: **Abscisic acid.** Its level rises when water is short. By **inhibiting growth**, it lets the sapling use less water and food, and it is linked with wilting and the closing of stomata, which cuts water loss. This helps the plant survive until it rains.

Nisha notices three things in her family’s kitchen garden. For each, name the plant hormone mainly involved and state whether it promotes or inhibits growth.

(a) A money plant on the windowsill has turned its stem towards the window.

(b) Young brinjals are swelling quickly as their cells divide.
