(a) **Auxin** — promotes growth (cells on the shaded side elongate).

(b) **Cytokinin** — promotes growth (cell division).

(c) **Abscisic acid** — inhibits growth (and causes wilting).

questions.solution_md: Identify the process in each case — bending towards light, cell division, wilting under water stress — and match it to the hormone.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Abscisic acid promotes the growth of the stem.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Abscisic acid inhibits growth; gibberellins help the stem to grow.

questions.stem_md: Iodine is needed by the body to make the hormone:

options.text_md: insulin
adrenaline
thyroxine
growth hormone

questions.solution_md: The thyroid gland uses iodine to make thyroxine — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Doctors find that a ten-year-old boy is much shorter than his classmates because his body makes too little growth hormone. Which gland is not working properly?

options.text_md: Thyroid gland
Adrenal gland
Pituitary gland
Pancreas

questions.solution_md: Growth hormone is secreted by the pituitary gland; too little in childhood causes dwarfism — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A stray bull suddenly charges at Kunal. His heart races, he breathes faster, and more blood flows to his leg muscles so that he can run. Which hormone causes these changes?

options.text_md: Insulin
Adrenaline
Thyroxine
Oestrogen

questions.solution_md: In an emergency the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and breathing and sends more blood to the muscles — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which hormone brings about changes such as a deeper voice and facial hair in boys at puberty?

options.text_md: Oestrogen
Thyroxine
Testosterone
Insulin

questions.solution_md: Testosterone, made by the testes, causes the changes of puberty in boys — option (c). Oestrogen does this in girls.

questions.stem_md:
A health camp in Lucknow measured the blood sugar of four adults after an overnight fast.

| Person | P | Q | R | S |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fasting blood sugar (mg/dL) | 88 | 96 | 168 | 79 |

A fasting value of 126 mg/dL or more, confirmed by a repeat test, suggests diabetes. Who should be sent for further tests, and which hormone is probably not acting properly?

options.text_md: R; insulin
S; insulin
R; adrenaline
P; thyroxine

Step 1 — Only R (168 mg/dL) is above 126 mg/dL.

Step 2 — High blood sugar suggests too little insulin, or cells not responding to it — option (a).

Step 3 — S has the lowest value (b); adrenaline (c) and thyroxine (d) are not the hormones that lower blood sugar.

questions.stem_md: A growth in a child’s hypothalamus damages it. Tests show that the pituitary gland itself is healthy, yet very little growth hormone is being released. Which explanation fits best?

options.text_md: The hypothalamus makes growth hormone, so none is being made.
The pituitary has started making insulin instead of growth hormone.
The hypothalamus normally breaks down extra growth hormone in the blood.
The hypothalamus can no longer send the releasing hormones that stimulate the pituitary.

Step 1 — The pituitary is healthy, so the problem is with the signal it receives.

Step 2 — The hypothalamus releases hormones that stimulate the pituitary to release growth hormone; without them, little growth hormone is released — option (d).

Step 3 — Growth hormone is made by the pituitary, not the hypothalamus (a); (b) and (c) describe things these glands do not do.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Diabetes can often be managed with injections of insulin.

**Reason (R):** Insulin is secreted by the adrenal glands.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

A is false, but R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The amount of insulin released falls when blood sugar returns to normal.

**Reason (R):** The release of many hormones is regulated by a feedback mechanism.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Falling insulin release as sugar returns to normal is an example of feedback control, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The hypothalamus helps to control the release of growth hormone.

**Reason (R):** The pituitary gland lies at the base of the brain.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the position of the pituitary does not explain why the hypothalamus controls growth hormone; that is because the hypothalamus releases hormones that stimulate the pituitary — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A hormone acts only on the gland that releases it.

**Reason (R):** Hormones are carried by the blood to target cells away from the gland.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: hormones act on target cells elsewhere in the body. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Endocrine glands release their hormones directly into the blood.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Endocrine glands are ductless; their hormones pass directly into the blood.

questions.stem_md: A lack of iodine in the diet can cause ___, a swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck.
questions.solution_md: Without iodine the thyroid cannot make enough thyroxine and enlarges: **goitre**.

questions.stem_md: Match each gland in Column A with the hormone it secretes in Column B.

options.text_md: Pituitary
Thyroid
Pancreas
Adrenal

questions.solution_md: Pituitary → growth hormone (1 → s); thyroid → thyroxine (2 → q); pancreas → insulin (3 → p); adrenal → adrenaline (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: An adult needs about 150 micrograms of iodine a day. A packet of iodised salt states that it contains 30 micrograms of iodine in every gram of salt. How many **grams** of this salt would supply one day’s iodine?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Iodine needed $= 150\ \mu\text{g}$; iodine per gram of salt $= 30\ \mu\text{g}$.

Step 2 — Mass of salt $= \dfrac{150}{30} = 5$, so about $5\ \text{g}$ of salt a day.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by a feedback mechanism in the control of hormones? Explain with the example of insulin and blood sugar.

answer.model_answer_md: In a feedback mechanism, the **level** of a substance controls how much hormone is released, so that the timing and amount of the hormone are just right. When blood sugar rises after a meal, cells of the pancreas detect it and release **more insulin**. As blood sugar falls back to normal, **insulin release is reduced**.

questions.solution_md: Define feedback, then describe both halves of the loop: more insulin when sugar is high, less when it is normal.

questions.stem_md:
A doctor tells Mr Iyer that his pancreas is not producing enough insulin.

(a) What problem is he likely to have, and why?

(b) Why may he be advised to take insulin injections and to limit sugary food?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diabetes**: without enough insulin, glucose is not taken up properly by the cells, so his blood sugar stays high.

(b) Injected insulin does the job his pancreas cannot, lowering blood sugar. Limiting sugary food avoids sharp rises in blood sugar that his body cannot bring down.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Link low insulin to high blood sugar (diabetes).

Step 2 — Explain the two remedies in terms of blood sugar.

questions.stem_md:
A health survey in a hilly district finds that many people have a swelling in the front of the neck.

(a) Name the condition and the gland involved.

(b) Explain how a shortage in the diet leads to this condition.

(c) Suggest one public health measure to prevent it.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Goitre**; the **thyroid** gland.

(b) The thyroid needs **iodine** to make **thyroxine**. Soil and water in some hilly areas contain little iodine, so people’s diets lack it. The thyroid cannot make enough thyroxine and enlarges, causing the swelling.

(c) Make sure everyone uses **iodised salt**, for example through ration shops and awareness campaigns.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Swollen neck → goitre → thyroid.

Step 2 — Iodine shortage → too little thyroxine → enlarged gland.

Step 3 — Iodised salt.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Iodine needed for thyroxine; shortage enlarges the gland

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between nervous and hormonal coordination in animals.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Nervous coordination uses **electrical impulses** along neurons; hormonal coordination uses **chemical messengers** (hormones) carried in the blood. (2) Nerve messages are **very fast** and their effect is short-lived; hormones act **more slowly**, but their effect lasts longer. (3) Nerve impulses reach only the cells connected by nerves; hormones reach **all cells** through the blood, but only target cells respond.

questions.solution_md: Compare the type of message, speed and duration, and how widely the message reaches.

questions.stem_md:
Late one evening, Divya is walking home when a dog suddenly barks and runs at her. She jumps back at once, and for several minutes afterwards her heart keeps pounding.

(a) Which part of her response was controlled mainly by the nervous system, and which by a hormone? Explain.

(b) Name the hormone and the gland that releases it.

(c) Describe three changes the hormone causes in the body, and how each helps her face the danger.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Jumping back at once was controlled by the **nervous system**, which acts in a fraction of a second. The pounding heart that lasted for minutes was due to a **hormone**, which acts more slowly but for longer.

(b) **Adrenaline**, released by the **adrenal glands** on top of the kidneys.

(c) The heart beats faster, so more oxygen reaches the muscles. Small arteries around the digestive system and skin contract, so more blood goes to the skeletal muscles. Breathing becomes faster because the diaphragm and rib muscles contract more, so more oxygen is taken in. All three prepare her body to run or to defend herself.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Fast and brief means nerves; slow and lasting means a hormone.

Step 2 — Adrenaline from the adrenal glands.

Step 3 — Heart rate, diversion of blood, breathing — each linked to more energy for the muscles.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Nervous for the jump, hormonal for the lasting heartbeat, with reason
(c) Three changes, each with its benefit (1 each)

questions.stem_md:
(a) What are endocrine glands? Why are they called ductless glands?

(b) Name the hormone secreted by each of these glands and state one function of each: thyroid, pancreas, pituitary, testes.

(c) Explain, with an example, how a feedback mechanism controls the amount of a hormone released.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Endocrine glands make hormones, chemical messengers that act on target cells elsewhere in the body. They have no ducts and release their hormones **directly into the blood**, so they are called ductless glands.

(b) Thyroid — **thyroxine**: controls the use of carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Pancreas — **insulin**: lowers blood sugar. Pituitary — **growth hormone**: controls growth and development. Testes — **testosterone**: brings about the changes of puberty in boys.

(c) When blood sugar rises after a meal, the pancreas detects it and releases more insulin, which lowers the sugar. As the level returns to normal, insulin release is reduced. The level of sugar thus feeds back to control the amount of insulin.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Define endocrine glands and explain "ductless".

Step 2 — Four gland–hormone–function sets.

Step 3 — Both halves of the feedback loop.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Feedback explained with an example in both directions

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
In a science club in Pune, students tested how quickly they react. One student held a 30 cm ruler upright, just above a partner’s open thumb and finger, and let it go without warning. The partner caught it as fast as possible, and the distance the ruler fell before being caught was noted: the shorter the distance, the quicker the reaction. Each result is the average of five tries for the same student. The reaction time was worked out from the distance using a formula from the club’s physics teacher.

| Condition | Average distance fallen (cm) | Reaction time (s) |
|---|---|---|
| Alert, watching the ruler | 15 | 0.17 |
| Counting backwards aloud while watching | 24 | 0.22 |
| After ten practice rounds | 12 | 0.16 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) a voluntary action that needs the brain

**(b)** **Photoreceptors** in the eye (retina), because the partner sees the ruler begin to fall.

**(c)** (i) While counting aloud, the brain is busy with another task, so it takes longer to process the sight of the falling ruler and send instructions to the hand: the distance rose from 15 cm to 24 cm. With practice, the brain becomes better at this pathway, so the response is quicker and the distance fell to 12 cm.

**OR** (ii) The claim is wrong. The reaction time rises from 0.17 s to 0.22 s when the catcher is distracted and falls to 0.16 s with practice, so the brain must be involved: the eye signals the brain, which instructs the hand. Spinal reflexes do not depend on attention like this. Catching the ruler is a quick **voluntary** action.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The partner must see the ruler fall and decide to close the fingers: eye → brain → hand muscles. It is a voluntary action — option (b).

**(b)** The stimulus is seen, so the receptors are in the eye.

**(c)** (i) From the table, the distance rose from 15 to 24 cm when distracted and fell from 15 to 12 cm after practice; link each change to the time the brain takes to process the signal and respond.

(ii) Point out that the time depends on attention and practice, which means the brain is involved, so it is not a reflex.

a voluntary action that needs the brain
an involuntary action controlled by the medulla
a hormonal response caused by adrenaline

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain why the average distance was larger while counting backwards aloud, and smaller after practice.
